**Surah al-Qadr (Surah 97)**

There are two opinions concerning it.

The first is that it is Meccan. This was related by Abu Salih from Ibn 'Abbas.

The second is that it is Medinan. This was said by al-Dahhak and Muqatil. Al-Mawardi said: "The first is the view of the majority." Al-Tha'labi said: "The second is the view of the majority."

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, We sent it down⦈. It means the Qur'an. ﴿On the Night of Decree⦈. This is because it was sent down all at once on that night to Bayt al-‘Izza (the House of Honour), which is a house in the lowest heaven. We have mentioned this hadith at the beginning of our book. The pronoun in ﴿Indeed, We sent it down⦈ refers to something not previously mentioned. Al-Zajjaj said: "Its mention has already occurred in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Indeed, We sent it down during a blessed night⦈ [al-Dukhan: 3]."

As for ﴿Night of Decree⦈, there are five opinions regarding why it is so named.

The first: al-Qadr means greatness, from your saying, "So-and-so has qadr (standing/esteem)." This was said by al-Zuhri. His saying, exalted is He, supports it: ﴿They did not measure God with His true measure⦈ [al-An'am: 91; al-Zumar: 67].

The second: it derives from constriction (đīq), meaning it is a night in which the earth is constricted (tadiqu) by the angels who descend. This was said by al-Khalil ibn Ahmad. His saying, exalted is He, supports it: ﴿And whoever has his provision restricted for him⦈ [al-Talaq: 7].

The third: al-Qadr means decree (al-hukm), as though things are decreed (tuqaddaru) in it. This was said by Ibn Qutaybah.

The fourth: because whoever had no standing becomes one of standing by observing it. This was said by Abu Bakr al-Warraq.

The fifth: because a Book of standing was sent down in it, and mercy of standing descends in it, and angels of standing (are present). This was related by our shaykh, 'Ali ibn 'Ubayd Allah.

They also differed on whether it is throughout the whole year or in Ramadan.

There are two views on this.

The first: it is in Ramadan. This is the view of the majority.

The second: it is throughout the whole year. This was said by Ibn Mas'ud.

Those who hold that it is in the month of Ramadan differed on whether it is restricted to a particular part of it, to the exclusion of others. There are two views.

The first: it is in the last ten (nights). This is the view of the majority, and most of the sound hadiths indicate it.

Al-Bukhari related in his Afrad (collection of single narrations) from the hadith of Ibn 'Abbas, from the Prophet ﷺ, that he said: "Seek it in the last ten (nights) of Ramadan, on the ninth remaining, or the seventh remaining, or the fifth remaining." In the hadith of Abu Bakrah, he said: "I do not seek it except in the last ten (nights), for a thing I heard from the Messenger of God ﷺ. I heard him say: 'Seek it on the ninth remaining, or the seventh remaining, or the fifth remaining, or the third remaining, or the last night.'"

The second view: it is in all of Ramadan. This was said by al-Hasan al-Basri.

Those who hold that it is in the last ten (nights) differed on whether it is restricted to the odd nights (al-witr) to the exclusion of the even nights (al-shaf'). There are two views.

The first: it is restricted to the odd nights. This is the view of the majority, and all the sound hadiths indicate it. Al-Bukhari and Muslim in the two Sahihs related from the hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, from the Prophet ﷺ, that he said: "Seek it in the last ten (nights), in the odd ones of them."

The second: it occurs in the even nights as it occurs in the odd nights. This was said by al-Hasan. It was related from al-Hasan and Malik ibn Anas that they both said: it is the night of the eighteenth.

Those who hold that it is in the odd nights differed on which of the odd nights is most specifically it, according to five opinions.

The first: the most specific is the night of the twenty-first. Al-Bukhari and Muslim in the two Sahihs related from the hadith of Abu Sa'id al-Khudri, who said: "The Messenger of God ﷺ observed seclusion (i'tikaf) in the middle ten (nights), and we observed seclusion with him. When we woke on the morning of the twentieth, he returned, and we returned with him. He was shown the Night of Decree, then it was made to be forgotten by him. He said: 'I saw the Night of Decree, then I was made to forget it, and I saw myself prostrating in water and mud. Whoever observed seclusion, let him return to his place of seclusion.' The sky became overcast on us at the end of that evening, and the roof of the mosque was of palm fronds, so the mosque leaked. By Him who is more honourable than that, and who sent down the Book to him, I saw him leading prayer; he began the Maghrib (prayer) on the night of the twenty-first, and his forehead and the tip of his nose were in the water and mud." This is the school of al-Shafi'i.

The second: the most specific is the night of the twenty-third. Abu Hurayrah related that the Prophet ﷺ said on the night of the twenty-third: "Seek it tonight."

Ibn 'Umar related from the Prophet ﷺ that he said: "Whoever among you wishes to perform some night prayer in the month, let him pray on the night of the twenty-third."

Muslim in his Afrad related from the hadith of 'Abd Allah ibn Unays that the Messenger of God ﷺ said: "I was shown the Night of Decree, then I was made to forget it, and I saw myself in the morning of it prostrating in water and mud." He said: "We were rained upon on the night of the twenty-third, and the Messenger of God ﷺ led us in prayer and then turned away, and the traces of water and mud were on his forehead and nose." He said: "'Abd Allah ibn Unays used to say: it is the night of the twenty-third."

The third: it is the night of the twenty-fifth. Abu Bakrah related this meaning from the Prophet ﷺ.

The fourth: it is the night of the twenty-seventh. Muslim in his Afrad related from the hadith of Ibn 'Umar, from the Messenger of God ﷺ, that he said: "Whoever is seeking it, let him seek it on the night of the twenty-seventh," meaning the Night of Decree. This is the view of 'Ali, Ubayy ibn Ka'b (who used to swear without making an exception that it is the night of the twenty-seventh), Ibn 'Abbas, 'A'ishah, and Mu'awiyah. Ahmad, may God be pleased with him, chose it.

It was related from Ibn 'Abbas that he deduced this from two things.

The first: he said that God, exalted is He, created man in seven categories, pointing to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We certainly created man from an extract of clay⦈ [al-Mu'minun: 12] and what follows. Then He made his provision in seven categories, pointing to His saying, exalted is He: ﴿That We poured down water in torrents⦈ [‘Abasa: 25]. Then Friday prayer is performed at the end of seven days, and He made the heavens seven, the earths seven, and the oft-repeated (al-mathani) seven. So I do not see the Night of Decree except as the seventh (night) [of the last ten, i.e., the twenty-seventh].

The second: he said that His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Peace⦈ is the twenty-seventh word, which indicates that it is so.

Some scholars argued: the Night of Decree is mentioned three times in this surah, and it consists of nine letters. Nine multiplied by three is twenty-seven. This is an indication of that.

The fifth opinion: the preferable thing is to seek it on the first night of Ramadan. This was said by Abu Razin al-‘Uqayli.

Ayyub related from Abu Qilabah that he said: "The Night of Decree moves around within the last ten (nights)."

As for the wisdom in concealing it, it is so that the diligence of the servants in the nights of Ramadan may be realized, out of hope of attaining it. Likewise, (God) concealed the hour of Friday, the hour of the night, His greatest Name, the middle prayer, and the Friend (wali) among people.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And what will make you know what the Night of Decree is?⦈ This is in the manner of magnification and of longing for its goodness.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The Night of Decree is better than a thousand months⦈. Mujahid said: its standing in prayer and its good deeds are better than the standing (in prayer) of a thousand months in which there is no Night of Decree, and its fasting. This is the saying of Qatadah, and the choice of al-Farra', Ibn Qutaybah, and al-Zajjaj. ‘Ata' related from Ibn 'Abbas that a man from the Children of Israel was mentioned to the Prophet ﷺ who carried weapons upon his shoulder in the way of God for a thousand months. The Messenger of God ﷺ was amazed at that and wished that this might be (granted) to his community. So God gave him the Night of Decree, and He said: it is better than a thousand months in which the Israelite carried weapons in the way of God. Some exegetes mentioned that in the past a man did not deserve to be called a worshipper until he worshipped God for a thousand months.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The angels and the Spirit descend therein⦈. Abu Hurayrah said: the angels on the Night of Decree on earth are more than the number of pebbles.

Regarding "the Spirit," there are three opinions.

The first: it is Jibril (Gabriel). This is the view of most. In the hadith of Anas, the Messenger of God ﷺ said: "When it is the Night of Decree, Jibril descends with a host of angels, who pray for and greet every servant standing or sitting who remembers God, mighty and majestic."

The second: the Spirit is a group of angels whom the (other) angels do not see except on that night. They descend from the setting of the sun until the rising of dawn. This was said by Ka'b and Muqatil ibn Hayyan.

The third: it is a great angel who equals a company of angels. This was said by al-Waqidi.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿therein⦈, that is, in the Night of Decree, ﴿by the permission of their Lord⦈, that is, by what He commanded and decreed, ﴿concerning every matter⦈. Ibn Qutaybah said: that is, with every matter. The exegetes said: they descend with every matter that God decreed in that year until the next. Ibn 'Umar, Ibn 'Abbas, Abu al-'Aliyah, and Abu 'Imran al-Jawni read: "min kulli imri'" (from every man), with a kasrah on the ra' followed by a hamzah with kasrah and tanwin, and with the lam joined without hamzah. This reading has two meanings.

The first: "From every angel, peace."

The second: "min" is in the sense of "‘ala" (upon). Its sense: upon every man among the Muslims is peace from the angels, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We aided him against the people who denied⦈ [al-Anbiya': 77]. The reading that conforms to the script of the Mushaf is the correct one. The completion of the speech is at His saying, exalted is He: ﴿concerning every matter⦈, then He began: ﴿Peace it is⦈, that is, the Night of Decree is peace. There are two views on the meaning of peace.

The first: no sickness occurs in it, and no devil is sent forth in it. This was said by Mujahid.

The second: the meaning of peace is good and blessing. This was said by Qatadah. Some scholars used to say: the pause on "Peace" (salam) is with the meaning that the angels descend with peace.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Until the emergence (matla') of dawn⦈. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', 'Asim, Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir, and Hamzah read "matla'i" with a fathah on the lam. al-Kisa'i read it with a kasrah. al-Farra' said: the fathah is stronger according to the analogy of Arabic, because "matla'" with a fathah is the rising, and with a kasrah is the place from which it rises. However, the Arabs say: "The sun rose matla'an," with a kasrah, while they mean the verbal noun, as you say: "I honoured you with karamah," and so you dispense with the noun for the verbal noun. We explained this meaning in "al-Kahf" at His saying, exalted is He: ﴿the rising place of the sun⦈ [al-Kahf: 90 / note: as given] with a sufficient explanation, and praise be to God.

The second: he said that His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Peace⦈ is the twenty-seventh word, which indicates that it is so.

Some scholars argued: the Night of Decree is mentioned three times in this surah, and it consists of nine letters. Nine multiplied by three is twenty-seven. This is an indication of that.

The fifth opinion: the preferable thing is to seek it on the first night of Ramadan. This was said by Abu Razin al-‘Uqayli.

Ayyub related from Abu Qilabah that he said: "The Night of Decree moves around within the last ten (nights)."

As for the wisdom in concealing it, it is so that the diligence of the servants in the nights of Ramadan may be realized, out of hope of attaining it. Likewise, (God) concealed the hour of Friday, the hour of the night, His greatest Name, the middle prayer, and the Friend (wali) among people.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And what will make you know what the Night of Decree is?⦈ This is in the manner of magnification and of longing for its goodness.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The Night of Decree is better than a thousand months⦈. Mujahid said: its standing in prayer and its good deeds are better than the standing (in prayer) of a thousand months in which there is no Night of Decree, and its fasting. This is the saying of Qatadah, and the choice of al-Farra', Ibn Qutaybah, and al-Zajjaj. ‘Ata' related from Ibn 'Abbas that a man from the Children of Israel was mentioned to the Prophet ﷺ who carried weapons upon his shoulder in the way of God for a thousand months. The Messenger of God ﷺ was amazed at that and wished that this might be (granted) to his community. So God gave him the Night of Decree, and He said: it is better than a thousand months in which the Israelite carried weapons in the way of God. Some exegetes mentioned that in the past a man did not deserve to be called a worshipper until he worshipped God for a thousand months.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿The angels and the Spirit descend therein⦈. Abu Hurayrah said: the angels on the Night of Decree on earth are more than the number of pebbles.

Regarding "the Spirit," there are three opinions.

The first: it is Jibril (Gabriel). This is the view of most. In the hadith of Anas, the Messenger of God ﷺ said: "When it is the Night of Decree, Jibril descends with a host of angels, who pray for and greet every servant standing or sitting who remembers God, mighty and majestic."

The second: the Spirit is a group of angels whom the (other) angels do not see except on that night. They descend from the setting of the sun until the rising of dawn. This was said by Ka'b and Muqatil ibn Hayyan.

The third: it is a great angel who equals a company of angels. This was said by al-Waqidi.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿therein⦈, that is, in the Night of Decree, ﴿by the permission of their Lord⦈, that is, by what He commanded and decreed, ﴿concerning every matter⦈. Ibn Qutaybah said: that is, with every matter. The exegetes said: they descend with every matter that God decreed in that year until the next. Ibn 'Umar, Ibn 'Abbas, Abu al-'Aliyah, and Abu 'Imran al-Jawni read: "min kulli imri'" (from every man), with a kasrah on the ra' followed by a hamzah with kasrah and tanwin, and with the lam joined without hamzah. This reading has two meanings.

The first: "From every angel, peace."

The second: "min" is in the sense of "‘ala" (upon). Its sense: upon every man among the Muslims is peace from the angels, like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And We aided him against the people who denied⦈ [al-Anbiya': 77]. The reading that conforms to the script of the Mushaf is the correct one. The completion of the speech is at His saying, exalted is He: ﴿concerning every matter⦈, then He began: ﴿Peace it is⦈, that is, the Night of Decree is peace. There are two views on the meaning of peace.

The first: no sickness occurs in it, and no devil is sent forth in it. This was said by Mujahid.

The second: the meaning of peace is good and blessing. This was said by Qatadah. Some scholars used to say: the pause on "Peace" (salam) is with the meaning that the angels descend with peace.

His saying, exalted is He: ﴿Until the emergence (matla') of dawn⦈. Ibn Kathir, Nafi', 'Asim, Abu 'Amr, Ibn 'Amir, and Hamzah read "matla'i" with a fathah on the lam. al-Kisa'i read it with a kasrah. al-Farra' said: the fathah is stronger according to the analogy of Arabic, because "matla'" with a fathah is the rising, and with a kasrah is the place from which it rises. However, the Arabs say: "The sun rose matla'an," with a kasrah, while they mean the verbal noun, as you say: "I honoured you with karamah," and so you dispense with the noun for the verbal noun. We explained this meaning in "al-Kahf" at His saying, exalted is He: ﴿the rising place of the sun⦈ [al-Kahf: 90 / note: as given] with a sufficient explanation, and praise be to God.
